source.title: On the importance of single directions for generalization
source.authors: Ari S. Morcos; D. G. Barrett; N. Rabinowitz; M. Botvinick

record.tranche_reason: Measures activation-space ablation and noise sensitivity as predictors of generalization across label corruption, models, training, and hyperparameters. These are different measures from the claim versions' specified sharpness measure and interventions.
record.gate_note: The study reports results on single-direction reliance and generalization, but does not test the specified versions: it does not measure the natural-label versus random-label held-out accuracy comparison, width beyond interpolation, architecture comparisons, optimizer comparisons, large-batch effects, test-error effects of dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or removal of memorized examples. Cited prior-work results are not extracted as rows.
record.test_reason: The study tests V1's memorization-capacity component in additional architectures and datasets: Section 3.1 explicitly reports approximately perfect training accuracy for all tested networks, including randomized-label conditions. It does not establish the complete natural-label versus random-label held-out comparison. Its main activation-ablation findings test none of V1–V8.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors associate better generalization with lower reliance on activation-space directions, propose ablation robustness as a model-selection signal, and find that batch normalization discourages reliance while class selectivity poorly predicts importance. They leave broader datasets and distribution-shift generalization for future work.
record.recipe_differences: Uses activation-space unit or feature-map ablations and normalized activation noise to study reliance on directions; does not use the claim versions' weight-perturbation sharpness measure or their specified interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: Label corruption fraction; ablation ordering; ablation value (zero versus empirical mean, with zero less damaging); dropout fraction; batch normalization; training time; hyperparameter settings; layer depth.

fits_no_version.finding: Corrupted-label networks are more sensitive to activation ablation and normalized activation noise; activation-ablation area also tracks generalization across natural-label networks, training time, and hyperparameters.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reliance on activation-space directions predicts generalization in the tested settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Dropout provides ablation robustness mainly up to its training fraction; batch normalization increases robustness, reduces class selectivity, and increases feature-map mutual information.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dropout and batch normalization affect activation-space reliance and information distribution differently.

fits_no_version.finding: Class selectivity and mutual information generally predict ablation importance poorly; class selectivity is unrelated or negatively related to filter L1 norm.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Individual-unit selectivity is generally a poor indicator of functional importance.

record.problems: Some generalization relationships are reported qualitatively or in figures without exact values. Corrupted-label experiments use training accuracy because those networks cannot generalize. The 200-network analysis notes a possible discrete regime shift but cautions it may reflect degeneracy in optimization solutions. Authors state further work is needed to evaluate the proxy on more complicated datasets and other generalization regimes.
record.rows_left_out: No additional result rows omitted; figure distributions and curves were retained only where the text explicitly describes the outcome, without estimating plotted values.

untested.parts: The complete coexistence comparison: natural-label held-out accuracy far above chance and randomized-label held-out accuracy at chance under matched recipes. No such paired held-out results are supplied. The original architectures and absence of explicit regularization are not reproduced throughout; ImageNet fit is reported using top-5 accuracy.
Width beyond interpolation and its effect on test error.
Controlled convolutional versus fully connected image-classification comparisons and local-connectivity interventions.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer generalization under specified tuning budgets.
Separate batch-size effects under fixed epochs and recipe adaptations.
Dropout's effect on held-out error, including dataset-size and augmentation conditions.
Magnitude-aware weight sharpness, generalization-gap ranking, and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized training examples, retraining, and comparison with random removal.

record.verdict_notes: The record's blanket statement that no version is tested overlooks the directly reported near-perfect training fits, which bear on V1's capacity component. Support for that component does not establish the full conjunction. States for rows linked to none are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8, without disputing their reported findings.

versions.untested_parts: Does not report held-out accuracy for natural-label versus random-label training; corrupted-label experiments use training accuracy.
No width sweep beyond the zero-training-error threshold.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
Dropout results concern ablation sensitivity and convergence, not held-out error reduction.
Measures activation-space reliance, not magnitude-aware weight perturbation sharpness or its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Does not remove memorized examples and retrain.

rows.subject: 2-hidden layer MLP

rows.operation_detail: Cumulative activation-space ablation of units, clamped to zero; performance measured by training accuracy on corrupted-label datasets.
rows.measure: Sensitivity of training accuracy to cumulative ablations
rows.value: Networks trained on corrupted labels were significantly more sensitive to cumulative ablations than those trained on true labels; curves were not always perfectly ordered by fraction corrupted.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 1 error bars: standard deviation across 10 random orderings of units to ablate.
rows.note: The text states the comparison and says curves begin at approximately 1 training accuracy and fall to chance when all directions are ablated; exact curve values are not stated.
rows.check: Only the unablated training-accuracy baseline bears on V1: approximately perfect fit includes randomized labels. The ablation-sensitivity contrast does not test V1. Chance accuracy after ablating all directions is not random-label held-out accuracy. The four listed widths refer respectively to different experiments, not four layers.

rows.subject: 2-hidden layer MLP
rows.operation_detail: Added Gaussian noise to units with zero mean and progressively increasing variance, normalized by each unit's empirical training-set activation variance.
rows.measure: Sensitivity to random-basis activation noise
rows.value: Networks trained on corrupted labels were substantially and consistently more sensitive to noise than those trained on true labels.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 2 error bars: standard deviation across 10 runs.
rows.note: Exact noise-response values are not stated.
rows.check: Activation-noise sensitivity measures neither V1's held-out comparison nor V7's magnitude-aware weight sharpness.

conditions.value: 200 with identical topology and data; varied initialization, data order, and learning rate
best 5 versus worst 5 by generalization error

rows.measure: Robustness of accuracy to cumulative ablation
rows.value: The 5 networks with the best generalization performance were more robust to ablation than the 5 with the worst generalization performance.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 3a error bars: standard deviation across 5 models and 10 random orderings of feature maps per model.
rows.note: The paper does not state exact curve values.
rows.check: Activation-ablation robustness versus generalization is a different construct from V7's weight-perturbation measure.

rows.subject: 11-layer convolutional network
rows.operation_detail: Measured normalized area under the cumulative ablation curve for each of 200 models and related it to generalization error.

conditions.value: 200 with identical topology and data; varied initialization, data order, and learning rate

rows.measure: Association between normalized ablation-curve area and generalization error
rows.value: Networks appeared to undergo a discrete regime shift in reliance; a negative correlation was also present within clusters.
rows.note: Authors caution that the apparent regime shift might be caused by degeneracy in the solutions found by optimization.
rows.check: The association concerns activation-ablation area, not any specified claim version.

rows.subject: MLP
rows.operation_detail: Tracked normalized area under the cumulative ablation curve, train loss, and test loss over training.
rows.measure: Association of ablation-curve area with test loss over training
rows.value: The point at which the area began to drop was the same point that train and test loss started to diverge; area and test loss had Spearman's correlation -0.728.
rows.note: The paper gives no confidence interval or p-value for the correlation.
rows.check: The activation-ablation proxy tests no version. Attribution is internally inconsistent: Section 3.2 describes an MNIST MLP, but Figure 4b's caption attributes the training correlation to a CIFAR-10 ConvNet; do not confidently combine both as one MNIST result.

rows.subject: ConvNet
rows.operation_detail: Measured normalized area under the cumulative ablation curve across a hyperparameter sweep.
rows.measure: Association between ablation-curve area and test accuracy
rows.value: Spearman's correlation 0.914; random subselections of 48 settings selected one of the top 1, 5, and 10 settings 13%, 83%, and 98% of the time; average test-accuracy difference from the optimal model was 1 ± 1.1% (mean ± std).
rows.note: Hyperparameters include learning rate and batch size, but the reported result is a proxy correlation and selection outcome, not separate effects of either parameter.
rows.check: Proxy correlation and hyperparameter-selection success do not measure a controlled batch-size effect. Selection-success percentages are method-performance results, not claim-effect rows.

rows.subject: MLP
rows.size_stated: 2-hidden layer; layer sizes 128, 512, 2048 and 2048 units for MNIST experiments
rows.operation_detail: Trained with dropout and measured cumulative-ablation sensitivity; networks with dropout on randomized labels were also evaluated for convergence.
rows.measure: Cumulative-ablation sensitivity relative to dropout fraction
rows.value: Both label conditions had minimal training-accuracy loss as single directions were removed up to the dropout fraction; past that point randomized-label networks were much more sensitive than unmodified-label networks. Unmodified-label networks with different dropout fractions were similarly robust.
rows.note: The stated outcome concerns ablation sensitivity, not held-out error. Dropout networks were reported to require more epochs to converge and to converge to worse solutions at higher probabilities.
rows.check: Dropout's ablation robustness and randomized-label convergence do not measure V6's held-out error reduction. The four widths refer respectively to different MNIST experiments; the dropout experiment uses width 2048.

rows.subject: Convolutional networks
rows.operation_detail: Compared cumulative-ablation robustness for training with and without batch normalization.
rows.measure: Robustness to cumulative feature-map ablation
rows.value: Networks trained with batch normalization were consistently and substantially more robust to these ablations.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 5b error bars: standard deviation across 4 model instances and 10 random orderings of feature maps per model.
rows.note: No exact curve values are stated.
rows.check: Batch-normalization effects on activation ablations test no specified version.

rows.subject: Convolutional networks
rows.operation_detail: Measured class-selectivity distributions for feature maps in networks trained with and without batch normalization.
rows.measure: Class selectivity of feature maps
rows.value: Networks trained without batch normalization exhibited a large fraction of feature maps with high class selectivity; class selectivity with batch normalization was substantially lower.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 6 distributions comprise 4 model instances; no numeric uncertainty stated.
rows.note: The paper separately reports that batch normalization increases mutual information in feature maps; exact distribution values are not stated.
rows.check: Feature-map class selectivity tests no specified version.

rows.measure: Mutual information in feature maps
rows.value: Batch normalization increases mutual information present in feature maps.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 6 distributions comprise 4 model instances; no numeric uncertainty stated.
rows.note: Exact distribution values are not stated.
rows.check: Feature-map mutual information tests no specified version.

rows.subject: MLP
rows.size_stated: 2-hidden layer; layer sizes 128, 512, 2048 and 2048 units for MNIST experiments
rows.operation_detail: Related unit class selectivity to the test-loss impact of ablating that unit.
rows.measure: Spearman correlation between class selectivity and ablation impact
rows.value: Spearman's correlation: 0.095; many highly selective units had minimal impact when ablated.
rows.note: Authors describe the correlation as slight but minor.
rows.check: Selectivity versus unit-ablation importance tests no specified version. The four widths describe separate experiments; class-selectivity experiments use width 128.

rows.subject: Convolutional network
rows.operation_detail: Related feature-map class selectivity to ablation impact across layers.
rows.measure: Relationship between class selectivity and feature-map importance
rows.value: Across layers, highly selective feature maps were no more impactful to ablate than non-selective maps; correlation was negative, Spearman's correlation -0.428.
rows.note: The paper states that the negative correlation was driven mostly by early layers; later layers showed no relationship.
rows.check: The negative selectivity–importance correlation is not a reversal of any specified version.

rows.subject: 50-layer ResNet
rows.operation_detail: Related feature-map class selectivity to ablation impact across layers.
rows.measure: Relationship between class selectivity and feature-map importance
rows.value: Across layers, ablation of highly selective feature maps was no more impactful than ablation of non-selective feature maps.
rows.note: Layer-specific results are displayed in Figure 7e; exact correlation values are not stated.
rows.check: Selectivity versus feature-map importance tests no specified version. Section 3.4 describes the ablation-impact measure as test loss; the record's top-5 condition should not automatically replace that measure.

rows.note: This is a related selectivity comparison, not a direct generalization-gap measure.
